title: Dyeing with elder leaves
subtitle: A warm yellow-green from elderberry foliage on alum-mordanted wool
excerpt: Elder leaves gathered in early summer give a warm yellow-green on alum-mordanted wool. The colour is stronger than many hedge-plant dyes because elder leaves have a good tannin and flavonoid content. The same tree that gives purple from its berries gives yellow-green from its leaves.
sourceNotes: Pellew, Dyes and Dyeing (1913), Internet Archive. Pellew lists elder (Sambucus) foliage among plants giving useful yellow-green shades on mordanted wool. Hummel, The Dyeing of Textile Fabrics (1885), Internet Archive, covers the alum mordant procedure.

glossaryTerms.definition: A metallic salt that bonds to wool fibre and provides attachment sites for plant dye molecules, improving colour fastness and depth.
Potassium aluminium sulphate, the standard beginner mordant for natural dyeing. Safe to use at home and gives clear, warm colours.

Naturally occurring plant compounds that bind to protein fibres. In dyeing, tannin pre-treatment helps plant-based dyes bond to cotton and linen, which lack the protein surface that mordants attach to on wool.

attrs.title: Mordant safety
attrs.body: Dye-pot work outdoors or in a ventilated kitchen. Dedicated pot and utensils only. Gloves and apron. Alum bath can compost after use.

attrs.title: Dye-plant cross-reference
attrs.body: Elder (Sambucus nigra) is a common British hedgerow tree. See the Garden tutorial on growing elder for foraging guidance.

items.name: Fresh elder leaves (collected in early summer)
items.qty: equal weight to the fibre being dyed

content.text: Dissolve alum in hot water and add to a pot of warm water. Enter the pre-wetted wool at 40°C, raise slowly to 80°C over 30 minutes, hold for 45 minutes, then let the pot cool. Either use the mordanted fibre immediately or leave it to soak overnight in the mordant bath. Rinse lightly before entering the dye-bath.

Pack the elder leaves into the dye-pot with enough water to cover the fibre freely. Bring the bath to 80°C and simmer for 45 to 60 minutes until the water is a deep yellow-green. Strain out the leaves and return the liquid to the pot. If the bath looks pale, add more leaves and re-extract.

Enter the mordanted fibre into the dye-bath at 40°C. Raise slowly to 80°C and hold for 60 minutes, turning the fibre every 15 minutes. Let the bath cool with the fibre in it for an extra 30 minutes before removing. Rinse in warm water and dry in shade. Elder-leaf yellow-green is brighter and more saturated than most hedge-plant dyes.

An iron modifier after-bath deepens the yellow-green to olive-green. Add a small amount of dissolved iron to a fresh warm-water bath, enter the dyed fibre, hold at 60°C for 15 minutes, rinse well. A copper modifier shifts the colour toward a brighter, truer green; see the copper mordant entry for wastewater disposal guidance, as copper baths require more careful disposal than alum.

items.problem: The colour is yellowish rather than yellow-green
items.cause: The leaves were too mature at harvest, or the dye-bath ran too hot and the colour compounds degraded
items.fix: Harvest leaves earlier in summer and keep the dye-bath below 85°C. Younger leaves from elder give a truer green-yellow.

items.problem: The colour is uneven across the skein
items.cause: The mordant or dye-bath was entered too hot, or the fibre was not turned regularly in the bath
items.fix: Enter the dye-bath from cool and raise slowly. Turn the fibre every 15 minutes to expose all surfaces to the bath evenly.
